content.title: Review
content.review:
Summary
-------

This paper proposes an approach to learning from large-scale webly-supervised video data for action recognition. Rather than training directly on the noisy web videos, a teacher model - trained on the target data - is used to identify alignment between the teacher and the noisy labels. Three reduced sub-pseudo label approaches are outlined to deal with clips that might not show the noisy web label. Experiments on existing datasets combined with new web videos show the potential of the proposed approach.

Strengths
---------

The notion of sub-pseudo labels is interesting and intuitive. In web videos, likely only a part of the long video shows the actual action, with the rest being noise. The ability to filter out such noise can boost video recognition from large-scale noisy sources.

The paper is clearly presented and comes with many experiments. Performing video experiments at scale is quite time-consuming, so the experiments are appreciated and help with understanding the pros and cons of the proposed approach and baselines. Figure 3 also helps with directly understanding the proposed variants and their relation to the baselines.

Weaknesses
----------

A limitation of the proposed approach is that it is not possible to use arbitrary web videos for pre-training. The label spaces of D_t and D_p need to be identical to construct confusion matrix C. This is a restrictive setup and not of high practical value. More commonly, a model is trained on an arbitrary large-scale web video dataset, after which a parameter transfer is performed to any dataset. In the proposed setup, for each new target set D_t, a new web set D_p needs to be constructed. See for example the source set of (Ghadiyaram et al., 2019).

The limitation listed above also creates a problem with the experimental evaluation. For example, the comparison to (Ghadiyaram et al., 2019) is presumably done using the same D_p. This is however not fair to the baseline, as this baseline is not restricted in their choice of D_p. How does this baseline perform when using their proposed source set?

Overall, the novelty of the paper is limited. Compared to current webly-supervised approaches, the proposed approach can assign sub-labels (Section 3.2) and then reduce the space of the sub-labels in three straight-forward ways (Section 3.3). While the simplicity of the approach is not negative at all (as it will enable a quicker integration into the field for one), the combination of limited technical novelty paired with modest improvements and a more restricted setup than baselines makes the paper low on impact overall.

A number of other questions remain as well in the experiments:
- What is the setup for HMDB51 and UCF101? Is K200 the target set for these datasets too?
- Idem for SoccerNet, is SoccerNet the base network here, or K200? It is hard to extract the information from the text.
- Why is Weak Label Train 82.8 in Table 1 and 83.9 in Table 2, even though Table 2 is with synthetic noise? Is it because the pre-training set is larger in Table 2?
- If yes to the question above, the big question is: what does the comparison look like when using more clips in Table 1? Running many experiments on large dataset is understandably difficult, but the picture from current experiments is that the difference with current approaches disappears when using a larger D_p.

Conclusion
----------

The paper presents a clear approach towards webly-supervised video action recognition. The notion of sub-pseudo labels is interesting and helps the recognition performance. There are however a number of pressing limitations, most notably regarding the strong limitation in the setup of D_p, subsequent restrictions to baselines in comparisons, and overall novelty of the paper. For the rebuttal, please address the concerns listed in the weaknesses.

content.title: Augments about the setup constraints.
content.comment:
Setup. Actually the most effective pre-training set IG-Kinetics in (Ghadiyaram et al., 2019) is actually constructed based on label space of Kinetics dataset rather than arbitrary web videos.  In terms of the generalization ability of the pre-trained representations by SPL (transfering model parameters to downstream datasets), our method does not have extra restrictions compared with (Ghadiyaram et al., 2019) for this part. Once the pre-training is finished using SPL on any pre-training set, e.g. WebK200 in our paper or IG-Kinetics in (Ghadiyaram et al., 2019), the pre-trained weights can still be transferred to any dataset. We validate this by following recent works e.g. WVT (Stroud et al., 2020), MIL-NCE (Miech et al., 2020) to conduct experiments on HMDB-51 and UCF-101 without building a new pre-train set specifically for them. The pre-training set is still WebK200, which is constructed based on class names from K200 (please check 4.2 WEAKLY-LABELED DATA COLLECTION section for details). We directly fine-tune the WebK200 pretrained model on HMDB-51 and UCF101 to show our learned representation is transferable and highly effective. Please note that in this experiment SPL pre-training is conducted on web data from different domains. 

When Web data and the Teacher model have different label space. it would be an interesting question to explore in the future for SPL as well as for general teacher-student frameworks. From our understanding of SPL, if this teacher model can provide some reliable knowledge/concept, we can rely on its knowledge to discover subclasses for each original query class. For web videos retrieved from the same query class, we can conduct teacher predictions on them and do statistics analysis for the teacher model predictions/logits. If we can find clear cluster characteristics for the teacher predictions/logits, we can divide the original query class into several subclasses based on this cluster information and provide enriched supervision. There will be new designs for assigning SPL accordingly. Meanwhile, we kindly argue that this is an open challenging question for general teacher-student frameworks. And our SPL can provide a direction to explore in the future.


Misc. questions:
+ Setup for HMDB51 and UCF101. The pre-training set is WebK200, which is constructed based on class names from K200 (please check 4.2 WEAKLY-LABELED DATA COLLECTION section for details). We do not construct new pre-training sets for HMDB-51 and UCF101. Instead we directly fine-tune the WebK200 pretrained model on HMDB-51 and UCF101 to show our learned representation is general and useful.
+ Setup for SoccerNet. SoccerNet is the name of the dataset for football which is proposed for action event recognition in soccer broadcast videos. The pre-training is conducted on WebS4 which is constructed based on class names of SoccerNet (check 4.2 WEAKLY-LABELED DATA COLLECTION section). 
+ Why is Weak Label Train 82.8 in Table 1 and 83.9 in Table 2. They are based on using different numbers of clips for pretraining: 6.7 *10^5 clips in Table 1 and d 1.4 × 10^6 clips in Table 2. You can check these numbers from the corresponding Table titles.  
+ Clear Performance gap. The performance gap between SPL and Weak Label Train does not disappear when having large numbers of training data: 1.5 top-1 accuracy gap for 147K videos with 6.7 *10^5 clips, 1.0 top-1 accuracy gap on 147K videos with 1.4 × 10^6 clips and 1.3  top-1 accuracy gap on 285K videos with 1.4 × 10^6 clips.

content.title: Sub-pseudo labels for weak learning
content.review:
Summary 

The paper proposes a technique to improve action classification for the case that weakly labeled training samples are available, e.g. in form of search queries or tags, and that a pretrained 'teacher' model is available, that can also generate class labels on those data. In this case, instead of just training on weak labels only or on teacher labels only, the paper proposes to use subpseudo labels out of both modalities using different merging techniques with a binary merging turning out as giving the best performance. The evaluation is done on Kinetics-200, HMDB, UCF101, and SoccerNet with a pretraining on WebK200 and WebS4 resp.

Paper strength

- Overall the paper is able to present competitive results for the proposed method. Even when trained weakly with the same number of clips (Tab. 2), the subpseudo based training is able to outperform the weakly trained baseline.

- The paper provides an extensive ablation study on the proposed idea.

- The paper is well written and easy to follow.

Paper weakness

- I'm not sure how applicable the overall idea would be for everyday actions. Obviously, datasets like Kinetics, UCF101, and HMDB which are at least partly based on Youtube clips and also have a vocabulary that is easy to search for (in the end, this is how they were build) might profit from more data, even if it's just retrieved by search terms, but I'm not sure how this could be extended to data that does not fit this description e.g. Something-Something, Epic Kitchen etc. 

- As a related question in this line, would this still work if the teacher model would be from a different domain with different classes.

- I have a feeling that the overall theoretical novelty of this paper might be a too limited for a machine learning conference, as the major contribution, in my impression, lays in the merging of weak labels and teacher predictions, which is a nice idea, but does not come with any theoretical foundation at this point. 

Summary

Overall, I think that this is an interesting paper, but I'm not sure if it hits the mark for a major machine learning conference based on the points raised above.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

content.title: Applicability and theoretical contributions
content.comment:
We thank R2 for the reviews and valuable comments.

If data is hard to search. We appreciate the reviewer for raising such a valuable question. Actually, one basic assumption for pre-training on web videos is that the search query is closely related to the content of the retrieved videos so that these queries can be treated as weak labels to provide effective supervision during pre-training. We also notice that there could be data that does not fit this description, such as class names of Something-Something. We have discussed this challenge in A.5 of Appendix. However, dealing with such cases is an open challenging question, which is out-of-scope of this paper. Please note that most recent and popular work (Ghadiyaram et al., 2019, Stroud et al., 2020) for learning from web data all rely on this basic assumption to construct the pre-training set. Our method does NOT increase a new level of limitation than general frameworks/methods for learning from web data. For the cases of Something-Something and Epic Kitchen, the existing method still need to rely on other reliable search queries (e.g. class name of K700) to retrieve web data for large-scale pre-training and expect a good generalization ability of the learned representations (like the case how our pretrained representations from WebK200 web data can well be generalized to HMDB-51 and UCF-101.)  


If the teacher model is from different domains with different classes. This is an interesting question to explore in the future for SPL as well as for general teacher-student frameworks. From our understanding of SPL, if this teacher model can provide some reliable knowledge/concept, we can rely on its knowledge to discover subclasses for each original query class. For web videos retrieved from the same query class, we can conduct teacher predictions on them and do statistics analysis for the teacher model predictions/logits. If we can find clear cluster characteristics for the teacher predictions/logits, we can divide the original query class into several subclasses based on this cluster information and provide enriched supervision. There will be new designs for assigning SPL accordingly. Meanwhile, we kindly argue that this is an open challenging question for general teacher-student frameworks. And our SPL can provide a direction to explore in the future.

Theoretical novelty. We agree theoretical understanding is interesting, but lacking it shouldn't be the rejection point of a deep learning paper. We have witnessed many effective deep learning methods do not have strong theoretical justification so far. The idea of this paper is relatively practical and aims to solve large-scale weakly-supervised training problems.

content.title: SPL_Review
content.review:
This paper presents a webly-supervised model for video recognition. The key idea od the proposed approach is to exploit the noisy data obtained from queried web videos as a weak supervision signal by introducing the concept of Sub-Pseudo Labels (SPL). These SPL are then used in a knowledge distillation framework to learn video representations. Interesting results are reported on several popular datasets such as HMDB51 and UCF101.

Pros:
+ Overall, the paper is well written and easy to follow. The key ideas of this work (i.e. the SPL concept and the proposed knowledge-distillation architecture) are well presented and adequately supported by experiments.
+ The most relevant related works are clearly presented, although the experimental results are not fully convincing in comparing the proposed model to similar previous webly-supervised action recognition models.
+ Experimental results are reported on several public benchmarks and, in general, they are quite interesting and competitive with the state-of-the-art.

Cons:
- Although interesting, the framework is a bit incremental (especially w.r.t Xie et al. 2020). The integration of the proposed SPL within a knowledge distillation architecture seems novel, but the comparison to the closest previous works could be improved.
- Experimental results are interesting and the authors present results on several datasets. However, the comparison with similar webly-supervised frameworks is not fully convincing. In particular, there are several comparisons with other pre-training strategies, but it is hard to judge the effectiveness of the overall approach in comparison to other webly-supervised video understanding frameworks since there are no direct comparisons. 


Minor comments:
- The prior works are well presented and most of the recent relevant works are properly cited. However, learning video recognition models from web videos (and web images) has been studied by many researchers. There are some related works that have not been discussed that are definitely relevant to this work, in particular in regards of the major challenges related to transferring the noisy knowledge coming from the web for video understanding tasks:
C. Gan et al, "You Lead, We Exceed: Labor-Free Video Concept Learning by Jointly Exploiting Web Videos and Images", CVPR 2016
S. Yeung et al, "Learning to learn from noisy web videos", CVPR 2017
C. Rupprecht et al, "Learning without Prejudice: Avoiding Bias in Webly-Supervised Action Recognition", CVIU 2018
- The motivations underlying the choice of the various datasets used in the experiments should be presented more clearly.
- Section 4.6 is hard to follow; it's not clear to me what has been done here and how it relates to the prior works. It is nice to see how SPL generalizes to weakly-labeled images, but, as they stand, these preliminary experiments are briefly presented and not fully convincing.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

display_title: The novelty is the design of sub-pseudo labels rather than frameworks.

content.title: The novelty is the design of sub-pseudo labels rather than frameworks.
content.comment:
We thank R1 for the reviews and valuable comments.

Framework novelty:
We kindly argue that the focus of this method is NOT a new framework. We align with the popular teacher-student framework. Although previous literature has shown large-scale pre-training with weak labels can directly benefit, we demonstrate that SPLs can provide enriched supervision and bring much larger improvements. Our method is orthogonal to the existing teacher-student training frameworks and can be combined with them to improve interesting tasks. To the best of our knowledge, SPL is a new design of pseudo label method which has not been explored before.

Experimental results comparison:
In addition to comparison with other pre-training strategies on K200 dataset, we also report results on UCF-101 and HMDB-51 benchmarks to compare with recent state-of-the-art in this area including webly-supervised video understanding frameworks such as WVT (Stroud et al., 2020), MIL-NCE (Miech et al., 2020). Complete comparison with settings details can be found in Table 7 of the Appendix. We find SPL achieves competitive results by using a smaller number of videos to conduct the pre-training and improving upon a weaker baseline model compared with R(2+1)D and S3D-G initialized by ImageNet pre-train weights. It is also necessary to note that conducting totally direct comparisons between recent webly-supervised video understanding frameworks is usually hard. This is due to the public unavailable web data used in each work, e.g. IG65M (Alwassel et al., 2019, Ghadiyaram et al., 2019), WVT-70M (Stroud et al., 2020), huge cost of computation resources for extreme large-scale pre-training etc. 

Discussion of previous work: 
We appreciate your suggestions and will add discussions and references about mentioned works. 

Choice of datasets: 
Thanks for your suggestion. We will make motivations underlying the choice of the various datasets more clear. (1) K200: Studies (Xie et al., 2018) show that evaluations on K200 can be well generalized to the full Kinetics. Due to the lack of computation resources required for extreme large-scale pre-training when taking full Kinetics as the target dataset (e.g. IG65M (Ghadiyaram et al., 2019), WVT-70M (Stroud et al., 2020)), K200 results in an optimal choice for new algorithm explorations with a proper scale. (2) UCF-101 and HMDB-51: they are standard downstream benchmarks used to evaluate the quality of pre-training. We follow most existing works to conduct comparisons on these two benchmarks. (3) SoccerNet: in order to evaluate the effectiveness of SPL on fine-grained actions and one of the important application domains (sport video recognition), we conduct experiments on SoccerNet dataset. (4) Clothing1M:  We aim to generalize our SPL from videos to images to show that core idea of SPL is a general contribution and can be applied to different domains. 

Section 4.6: 
We want to generalize our method from videos to images. Clothing1M contains 47,570 training images with human-annotated labels and 1M images with noisy labels. Different methods are studied to utilize human-annotated to better train on large weakly-labeled web data. SPL can directly be used for this task. This setting is exact to the problem SPL is addressing, as we can use human-annotated data to train teacher models and pre-training models using SPL on the 1M images. Lastly, fine-tuning on the human-annotated images to test results.
